messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus's Story

Marcus was nineteen when the fever started. It came on a Tuesday in November, unremarkable at first—chills, fatigue, the kind of thing that might pass in a few days. By Friday, he was in the emergency department at County Hospital with a diagnosis that would fracture his sense of safety in his own body: acute leukemia. What followed was a blur of fluorescent lights, the plastic smell of antiseptic that seemed to coat his throat, and the endless procession of needles—blood draws, port placements, chemotherapy lines. He remembers the nurse's apologetic expression as she approached with the IV catheter, the sharp sting, the way his body went rigid with a panic he couldn't name. The hospital became a place where his body stopped being his own, where machines beeped warnings about his failing cells, where he learned that the thing keeping him alive was also poisoning him. The chemotherapy made him vomit until his ribs ached. His hair fell out in clumps. He was eighteen years old, and his body had become a war zone.

He survived. The leukemia went into remission after eight months of treatment, and he was discharged with a clean scan and instructions to follow up regularly. But something had shifted. Marcus had come to believe that his body could no longer be trusted—it had betrayed him once, catastrophically, and there was no guarantee it wouldn't do so again. Once he had settled into this conviction—that his body was fundamentally unreliable, a trap waiting to spring—nearly everything became a potential signal of danger. A flutter in his chest, a random ache, the beep of a microwave, even the sight of a hospital parking lot from the highway: all of these seized his attention now in ways they wouldn't have before, each one confirming what he already believed about himself. This conviction gnawed at him in ways he couldn't quite articulate. When he felt his heart rate climb, or noticed a new ache, he was certain it was the cancer returning, that his body was already betraying him again. The meaninglessness crept in alongside this fear. He'd been given a second chance, people said, but what did that even mean? He'd spent months in a hospital bed watching other patients not make it. He'd lost his senior year of high school to treatment. His friends had moved on without him. Nothing felt like it mattered anymore—not his grades, not his future, not even his relationship with his girlfriend, Emma, who had stuck by him through the worst of it.

Six months after discharge, Marcus took a job as a counselor at a youth crisis helpline. It seemed like the right thing—to turn his experience into something that could help others. But the triggers were everywhere, and they had a way of pulling him under. When a caller mentioned a hospital stay, Marcus found his heart hammering, his palms suddenly slick with sweat. The smell of antiseptic in the clinic's bathroom sent him spiraling. Each time these moments hit—a caller's mention of IV lines, the chemical sting in the air—Marcus would find himself leaving work early, calling in sick the next day, or rearranging his schedule to avoid the clinic bathroom altogether. The triggers had become so intolerable that he began structuring his entire day around the possibility of encountering them. Most unbearable were the moments when he had to sit with his own thoughts about what he'd been through—the therapy his oncologist had recommended, the support groups he'd attended. He began avoiding anything that required him to process what had happened. He wouldn't read his own medical records. He wouldn't talk to Emma about his fears. He stopped going to his follow-up appointments, convincing himself that if he didn't think about the illness, it couldn't touch him again. When his oncologist's office called to schedule his six-month scan, Marcus felt the old panic rise and simply didn't answer; when Emma suggested he look at his discharge summary, he left the room rather than face it. The avoidance felt protective, like a way of taking back control, but it fed something darker. The avoidance felt protective, like a way of taking back control, but it fed something darker.

His sleep deteriorated. He'd lie in bed, and the moment he closed his eyes, his body would jolt awake—convinced something was wrong, that he was back in the hospital, that the monitors were alarming. He started staying up deliberately, scrolling on his phone until two or three in the morning, anything to avoid that moment of surrender to sleep. When unexpected sounds came—a car door slamming outside his apartment, Emma moving quickly in the next room—his entire nervous system would spike, as if danger were imminent. His body reacted as if he were still in the hospital, still in crisis, even though he was safe at home. This hypervigilance exhausted him. Because his body kept signaling danger, and because he had come to see his body as fundamentally unreliable, he became more certain that something was wrong with him, that he was broken in ways no doctor could fix. This belief drove him further into avoidance—he couldn't bear to return to the hospital for his oncology checkups, couldn't face the possibility of bad news, couldn't sit with the dread that came with waiting rooms and the smell of disinfectant. The avoidance bought him temporary relief, but it also meant his sleep worsened, his startle response intensified, and the conviction that his body was his enemy deepened.

Emma noticed the change. She'd find him awake at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling. When she touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he'd flinch violently, as if she'd struck him. She asked him to go back to his oncologist for his six-month scan, and Marcus felt something collapse inside him. The thought of returning to that building, of lying in the imaging machine, of hearing the technician say they'd found something—it was unbearable. He told her he was fine, that he didn't need to go, that he felt healthy. But the truth was darker: he was terrified that if he went back, they would confirm what he already knew—that his body was a trap, that nothing in his life would ever be safe or meaningful again. At nineteen, Marcus carried the weight of a man who had stared down his own mortality and found himself unable to believe in recovery. It was only when Emma finally insisted, when she said she couldn't watch him disappear into avoidance anymore, that Marcus made an appointment with a trauma therapist. He sat in the waiting room, hands shaking, the fluorescent lights overhead making his skin crawl. He was terrified of what talking about it would mean, but he was also running out of places to hide.
